## Scope

The present review surveys 109 papers published over the last 9 years dealing with adsorbents for gas drying, that is to say, with the removal of water vapour from a gas stream by means of a solid material which takes up the water and is subsequently regenerated so that the process can be repeated in a cyclic fashion. The adsorbents falling within the scope of the review are the silica gels, the activated aluminas, the zeolite molecular sieves, and, increasingly in recent years, a variety of newer porous solids that have been proposed for the same duty. The gases concerned include natural gas, air, and a range of process gases, and the duties extend all the way from relatively modest drying requirements to the extremely low residual water contents demanded by downstream operations such as liquefaction and low-temperature separation. It should be noted at the outset that virtually all of the work reviewed is cyclic in character: the bed adsorbs under one set of conditions and is regenerated under another, whether by heating, by depressurisation, or by purging with dry gas, and it follows that the performance of an adsorbent in this literature is as much a property of the cycle in which it is employed as it is of the material itself.

## Established results

On the broad directions of the principal effects there is, happily, little disagreement. The uptake of water by all of the adsorbents under consideration increases as the partial pressure of water vapour in the gas increases, and decreases as the temperature increases, which is why drying is carried out cold and regeneration is carried out either hot or at reduced pressure. Water is bound strongly at the hydrophilic sites of these materials, far more strongly than the carrier gas, and it is this preferential binding that makes the separation feasible in the first place; by the same token, however, it makes regeneration the energy-intensive step of the cycle, since the water that is most readily adsorbed is inevitably the water that is most difficult to drive off again.

The outline of breakthrough behaviour is equally well established. A bed continues to dry the gas to its outlet specification until such time as the adsorption front reaches the outlet end of the bed, whereupon the water content of the outlet gas rises sharply. The useful capacity of a bed is accordingly the capacity up to breakthrough rather than the equilibrium capacity of the material, and it is eroded by anything that broadens the front, including excessive velocity, maldistribution, and channeling. There is also general agreement that capacity is progressively lost over repeated cycling, owing to contamination of the bed by heavier components present in the gas, to damage caused by liquid water reaching materials that liquid water harms, and to the gradual degradation of the pore structure under repeated heating, and furthermore that this loss is most rapid during the early life of a bed.

## Disagreements

Where the literature becomes considerably less harmonious is in the region of low partial pressure, where reports are in conflict over the equilibrium water uptake, the very quantity that determines how dry a gas a given adsorbent is capable of delivering. Values published for what is nominally the same class of material, at nominally the same temperature, differ from one another by more than the differences between the materials themselves, and rankings of materials constructed from data in this region have a disconcerting habit of reversing from one paper to the next.

A good deal of this conflict appears to arise because the quantity is not, in fact, being measured on material in the same state. Different laboratories regenerate their adsorbents under different conditions before measurement, and a sample that goes into the measurement still carrying residual water will inevitably report a lower uptake than the same sample fully regenerated. Equilibration at low partial pressures is a slow business, and some of the values in the literature are in reality uptakes recorded after a fixed waiting period rather than true equilibrium values. The measurement techniques differ too: gravimetric determinations, uptakes inferred from breakthrough curves, and volumetric measurements do not interrogate the bed in the same state, and each has its own sensitivity to the temperature control on which low-pressure uptake so critically depends. The disagreement is therefore, at least in part, a disagreement about the state of the material being measured, and until preparation and equilibration are reported on a common basis, the values published in this region cannot meaningfully be ranked against one another.

## Gaps

Perhaps the most striking omission in this literature is a measurement that nobody seems to report at all, namely the water uptake retained after extended regeneration cycling. The papers characterise fresh material: they give the equilibrium uptake, the breakthrough capacity, and the behaviour over at most a modest handful of cycles. Yet the quantity that a design actually consumes is the capacity of the bed after it has been regenerated many times over, under genuine plant conditions, exposed to genuine plant gas with all of its contaminants and its full thermal history, precisely the conditions that the laboratory cycle leaves out.

This gap is far from academic, because the established results demonstrate that capacity declines with cycling, and declines fastest early on, which is exactly the territory that a long cycling record would illuminate. In the absence of retained-uptake data over extended cycling, a designer who sizes a bed on the basis of fresh capacity has no way of knowing whether the ageing margin he has allowed is generous or inadequate, and an operator has no way of telling from the literature when the drying performance of a bed will approach its limit. The missing measurement is not a difficult one; it is merely a long one. Until it is reported, the low-pressure disagreement also remains open in practice, since some part of the scatter between papers may well be attributable to the unreported cycling histories of the materials that were measured.

## Scope

This review covers 109 papers from the last 9 years on adsorbents for gas drying: the removal of water vapour from a gas stream by a solid that takes the water up and is then regenerated so that the cycle can repeat. The adsorbents in scope are silica gels, activated aluminas, zeolite molecular sieves, and the newer porous solids reported for the same duty. The gases dried in the papers range across natural gas, air, and process gases, and the duties range from moderate drying to the very low residual water contents that downstream processes such as liquefaction and low-temperature separation demand. Almost all of the work is cyclic: a bed adsorbs at one set of conditions and is regenerated at another, by heating, by reducing the pressure, or by a purge of dry gas, and the performance of an adsorbent in this literature is a property of the cycle as much as of the material.

## Established results

The direction of the main effects is not in dispute. The uptake of water by every adsorbent in scope rises as the partial pressure of water in the gas rises and falls as the temperature rises, so drying is done cold and regeneration is done hot or at reduced pressure. Water is held strongly on the hydrophilic sites of these materials, much more strongly than the carrier gas is held, which is what makes the separation possible at all and also what makes regeneration the expensive step of the cycle: the water that is easiest to take up is the hardest to remove. The same strength of binding is what lets a bed dry a gas to very low residual water contents: the last water taken up is held on the strongest sites, and the outlet gas continues to dry as those sites are filled.

Breakthrough behaviour is likewise settled in outline. A bed dries the gas to its outlet specification until the adsorption front reaches the outlet, after which the outlet water content rises steeply; the useful capacity of the bed is the capacity up to breakthrough, not the equilibrium capacity of the material, and it is shortened by anything that spreads the front, including high velocity, poor distribution, and channeling. Studies agree that capacity is lost over repeated cycling, through contamination of the bed by heavier components in the gas, through liquid water reaching a material that liquid water damages, and through gradual loss of the pore structure under repeated heating, and that the loss is fastest early in the life of a bed.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure, the region that decides how dry a gas a given adsorbent can deliver. Values reported for the same class of material, at the same nominal temperature, differ by more than the differences between the materials themselves, and rankings of materials drawn from that region reverse between papers.

The papers disagree, in part, because the quantity is not measured in the same state. Adsorbents are regenerated before measurement under conditions that differ between laboratories, and an adsorbent that enters the measurement carrying residual water reports a lower uptake than the same adsorbent fully regenerated. Equilibration at low partial pressure is slow, and some reported values are uptakes after a fixed waiting time rather than equilibrium values. The measurement routes differ as well: gravimetric uptakes, uptakes inferred from breakthrough curves, and uptakes from volumetric instruments do not sample the same bed state, and each route has its own sensitivity to the temperature control that low-pressure uptake depends on. The conflict is therefore partly a conflict about the state of the material at measurement, and until the preparation and the equilibration are reported on a common basis, the published values in this region cannot be ranked against each other.

## Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the water uptake retained after extended regeneration cycling. Papers characterise fresh material: the equilibrium uptake, the breakthrough capacity, and the behaviour over a handful of cycles at most. The quantity a design actually consumes is the capacity of the bed after it has been regenerated many times under plant conditions, with plant gas, including the contaminants and the thermal history that the laboratory cycle omits.

The gap matters because the established results show that capacity falls with cycling and falls fastest early, which is exactly the region the long record would resolve. Without retained-uptake data over extended cycling, a designer sizing a bed on fresh capacity cannot tell whether the margin allowed for ageing is generous or inadequate, and an operator cannot tell from the literature when a bed's drying performance will reach its limit. Replacement is therefore decided on schedule or on deterioration at the outlet, not on capacity data, because the capacity data over the bed's working life do not exist. The missing measurement is not difficult; it is long. Until it is reported, the low-pressure disagreement also stays open in practice, since part of the spread between papers may be the unreported cycling history of the materials they measured.
